title: 370. Geometry, Spatial Thinking & Measurement: Surface Area and Volume of Spheres
description: A comprehensive mathematics curriculum progressing from foundational numeracy and core mathematical concepts to algebra, geometry, calculus, linear algebra, probability, statistics, discrete mathematics, optimization, mathematical foundations of AI, advanced pure mathematics, and emerging research methods.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate a sphere's surface area from its radius.
questions.question: A sphere has radius \(3\text{ cm}\). What is its surface area?
questions.explanation: The surface area is \(4\pi r^2=4\pi(3^2)=36\pi\text{ cm}^2\).
questions.hint: Recall how the radius enters the sphere-area formula.

questions.learningObjective: Calculate exact sphere volume from radius.
questions.question: A sphere has radius \(4\text{ cm}\). What is its volume?
questions.hint: Keep the fractional coefficient in the sphere-volume formula.

questions.learningObjective: Convert sphere diameter to radius before finding area.
questions.question: A sphere has diameter \(10\text{ m}\). What is its surface area?
questions.explanation: The radius is \(5\text{ m}\), giving \(4\pi(5^2)=100\pi\text{ m}^2\).
questions.hint: Determine the radius from the supplied diameter.

questions.learningObjective: Convert diameter to radius when computing sphere volume.
questions.question: A sphere has diameter \(6\text{ cm}\). What is its volume?
questions.explanation: The radius is \(3\text{ cm}\). Its volume is \(\frac{4}{3}\pi(27)=36\pi\text{ cm}^3\).
questions.hint: The cube in the formula applies to the radius.

questions.learningObjective: Recover a positive radius from sphere surface area.
questions.question: A sphere has surface area \(196\pi\text{ cm}^2\). What is its radius?
questions.explanation: The equation \(4\pi r^2=196\pi\) gives \(r^2=49\), hence \(r=7\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Divide out the surface-area coefficient before taking a square root.

questions.learningObjective: Recover a radius from an exact sphere volume.
questions.question: A sphere has volume \(\frac{500\pi}{3}\text{ cm}^3\). What is its radius?
questions.explanation: From \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3=\frac{500\pi}{3}\), we obtain \(r^3=125\), so \(r=5\text{ cm}\).
questions.hint: Isolate the cubed radius before taking a cube root.

questions.learningObjective: Subtract inner sphere volume from outer sphere volume.
questions.question: A hollow spherical shell has outer radius \(5\text{ cm}\) and inner radius \(3\text{ cm}\). What is the volume of its material?
questions.explanation: The material volume is \(\frac{4}{3}\pi(5^3-3^3)=\frac{4}{3}\pi(98)=\frac{392\pi}{3}\text{ cm}^3\). Cubing the thickness does not give the shell volume.
questions.hint: Subtract the volume of the hollow interior.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a hemisphere's curved area from its total area.
questions.question: A hemisphere has radius \(6\text{ cm}\). What is its curved surface area, excluding the flat circular face?
questions.explanation: The curved surface is half a sphere's surface: \(2\pi(6^2)=72\pi\text{ cm}^2\). Including the flat face would give \(108\pi\).
questions.hint: Decide which fraction of the original curved sphere surface remains.

questions.learningObjective: Use sphere-volume ratios to count smaller spheres.
questions.question: A solid sphere of radius \(6\text{ cm}\) is melted into identical solid spheres of radius \(2\text{ cm}\), with no material loss. How many smaller spheres are made?
questions.explanation: The count is the volume ratio \(\frac{6^3}{2^3}=27\). An area ratio would not conserve material volume.
questions.hint: Compare volumes rather than surface areas.

questions.learningObjective: Recover radius from area and then calculate volume.
questions.question: A sphere has surface area \(144\pi\text{ cm}^2\). What is its volume?
questions.explanation: First \(4\pi r^2=144\pi\) gives \(r=6\text{ cm}\). Then \(V=\frac{4}{3}\pi(6^3)=288\pi\text{ cm}^3\).
questions.hint: Find the radius before changing from an area formula to a volume formula.
